page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: What G is
lines: Gibbs energy G is a thermodynamic quantity
of a system: the energy available to do
useful work at constant temperature and
It is a state function, defined as G = H − TS.
steps.why: Of a system's total enthalpy, the part TS is tied to disorder and is not available as work; what remains, H − TS, is the usable part — the Gibbs energy. The energy available to do useful work is the board's standard wording for this, and it is the wording to write. What that wording is short for is the CHANGE: at constant temperature and pressure −ΔG equals the maximum non-expansion (useful) work the process can deliver. Only differences in G are measurable, which is why the second mark is the ΔG test rather than a value of G.
common_mistakes: Leaving out at constant temperature and pressure — those are the conditions that make G the right quantity.
Writing G = H + TS. The TS term is subtracted.
steps.memory_tip: G is the work-usable part of the enthalpy: H minus the tied-up part TS.

steps.label: Spontaneity criterion
lines: The change in G decides spontaneity at
ΔG = 0 : the system is at equilibrium

lines.text: ΔG negative: spontaneous. ΔG zero: equilibrium.

steps.why: ΔG combines the enthalpy change and the entropy change into one number whose sign gives the direction of the process, using system quantities only.
common_mistakes: Writing ΔG = ΔH + TΔS — the entropy term is subtracted.
Giving the signs without the equation, or the equation without the signs. Both halves are needed.
steps.memory_tip: Negative ΔG, natural direction: the three cases are minus, plus, zero for go, no, and balanced.
steps.margin_note: The equation and all three sign cases complete the answer.

insider_note: Explain here means three things in order: what G is, the equation ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, and the three sign cases. Answers that give only the equation lose the first mark.
